rawEventDetails: Speaker Christopher Burcham Affiliation University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign Details Event Description Crystal engineering has been used within the pharmaceutical industry for multiple decades, primarily applied to batch processes. Crystal engineering is employed for the control of crystal attributes such as crystal form, particle size, particle morphology as well as impurity rejection. While applied across intermediate steps, crystal engineering is often utilized for the isolation of the active pharmaceutical ingredient, as these particle attributes can directly impact the bioavailability of the drug when used in solid oral dosage forms. Concurrent with the increased utilization of particle engineering techniques, the pharmaceutical industry has also rediscovered continuous processing and as a natural result there has been an increased interest in continuous crystallization and isolation of pharmaceutical intermediates and APIs. Continuous crystallization presents unique challenges to the control of physical properties of active pharmaceutical ingredients by direct crystallization when compared to batch crystallization processes. These limitations can be overcome to some extent by the implementation of in-situ milling and other process intensification technologies. Development of these processes has historically been experiential through trial-and-error experimentation – which leads to long development cycles, and the need for significant quantities of materials to fund the development studies. Application and utilization of population balance models (PBM) significantly decrease both the development cycle time and the material needs – a case study demonstrating the efficiency gains of using PBMs will be presented. While the utilization of PBMs greatly decreases the development timeframe, the overall process development cycle is quite linear, such that the development of the process cannot begin until many other activities are completed, all of which rely on the selection of the crystal form that will be carried forward – which until recently has been done through extensive crystal screening studies. Innovations in ab-initio crystal structure predictions (CSP) offer the promise of transforming polymorph screening and selection by predicting all possible polymorphs of a given organic molecule along with the associated free energies of each predicted form. These advances in the ability to predict crystal form as well as crystal growth have progressed to such a point where one can ask – can the linear process development workflow be replaced through in-silico simulations? (Burcham et al, 2024). An in-silico workflow for the digital design of crystallization processes starting from the chemical structure of the active pharmaceutical ingredient (API) through to process development will be presented. The opportunities, current limitations and prospects for future innovation of this approach will be discussed. 1. Burcham, C. L., et al. (2024). "PharmaceuScal Digital Design: From Chemical Structure through Crystal Polymorph to Conceptual Crystallization Process." Crystal Growth & Design 24(13): 5417–5438.

rawEventDetails: Speaker Yaniv Romano Affiliation Technion- Israel Institute of Technology Details Event Description Abstract AI models are powerful, yet their use in practice raises two fundamental challenges. The first is trust: how can we make reliable inferences from black-box models when we only have a few reference examples to rely on? The second is steerability: how can we guide AI generation when we can recognize the outputs we prefer but cannot precisely quantify our preferences? In this talk, I will show how statistics and AI can empower one another to tackle both challenges. The first part focuses on reliable inference under limited data. I'll introduce General Synthetic-Powered Inference (GESPI), a framework that safely enhances the sample efficiency of any statistical inference procedure—such as conformal prediction and hypothesis testing—by adaptively leveraging synthetic data. GESPI provides distribution-free error control regardless of synthetic-data quality while improving utility when those data are informative. I'll demonstrate its applicability across domains ranging from predictive uncertainty quantification to principled win-rate evaluation of large reasoning models. I'll also discuss how these ideas can support large-scale scientific discovery with false discovery rate control. In the second part, I'll introduce Preference-based Metropolis-Hastings (Pref-MH): a model-steering framework that leverages pairwise votes from an LLM judge to generate data satisfying complex properties of interest. Pref-MH exploits a novel connection between MH and the Bradley-Terry preference model. This connection enables rigorous steering of a base AI generator toward a target distribution that favors outputs preferred by the judge, without ever needing to estimate the judge's latent reward. Finally, I'll demonstrate Pref-MH in molecular design and show how the resulting synthetic data improve downstream inference when incorporated into GESPI. His super-resolution technology, invented with Peyman Milanfar, has been integrated into Google’s flagship products, including Pixel phones. His uncertainty quantification method, developed with Emmanuel Candès, was used by The Washington Post to estimate outstanding votes during the U.S. presidential election. Yaniv has received several honors and awards, including an ERC Starting Grant, the SIAG/IS Early Career Prize, the Sheila Samson Prime Minister’s Prize (Researcher Recruitment Prize), the IEEE Signal Processing Society Best Paper Award, the Alon Scholarship, the Krill Prize for Excellence in Scientific Research, and the Henry Taub Prize for Academic Excellence. rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Abstract: Electrifying energy-intensive industries is a key component of reducing fossil fuel consumption and meeting decarbonization goals, but these end uses have been slower to transition than other sectors of the economy because of the diversity of industrial processes, the heat and temperature requirements involved, and the capital-intensive nature of existing infrastructure. The scale of transitioning this sector of the economy will also have significant impacts on the broader electricity sector, including changes in demand patterns, grid capacity requirements, and infrastructure investment needs, all of which need to be taken into account in order to evaluate the impact of industrial technologies. This seminar will introduce multiscale modeling frameworks used to analyze the impact of industrial electrification on the broader electricity system, from individual process-level changes up to system-wide effects, as well as the lifecycle analysis methods used to assess the environmental impacts of these electrified alternatives across their full value chain. In addition to the environmental impacts of industrial electrification, these methods also consider the impacts on energy prices and the cost of producing goods via electrified alternatives, offering a more complete picture of the economic trade-offs involved in this transition. Examples of industrial electrification pathways at different scales will be presented, including individual facilities with small and large energy demand, as well as broader scenarios considering the electrification of entire industrial sectors like the steel industry, illustrating how these modeling approaches can inform decision-making at both the facility and sector level. Prior to Purdue, she was a postdoctoral researcher at the Andlinger Center for Energy and the Environment. rawEventDetails: Speaker Trey Holley Details Event Description Inorganic cesium lead halide perovskites (CsPbX 3 , where X = I, Br) possess superior thermochemical stability compared to hybrid organic–inorganic perovskites, positioning them as highly promising candidates for long-term photovoltaic applications. However, their performance and commercial viability remain constrained by polymorphic instability, Pb-rich and Cs-rich defect formation, and challenging surface defect passivation. This dissertation systematically elucidates the processing–structure–property relationships that dictate polymorph stability, perovskite reaction kinetics, and optoelectronic behavior in all-inorganic halide perovskite thin films. First, to address the rapid transformation of photoactive black CsPbI 3 ( α, β, γ polymorphs) into the non-photoactive yellow polymorph ( δ -CsPbI 3 ), this work quantitatively investigates the reconstructive polymorph transformation kinetics. Utilizing in situ isothermal X-ray diffraction (XRD) and time-resolved optical microscopy, the polymorph transformation is modeled via Johnson–Mehl–Avrami–Kolmogorov (JMAK) kinetics, establishing that the transformation proceeds through an interface-controlled, thermally activated two-dimensional growth mechanism. The resulting Time-Temperature-Transformation (TTT) diagram serves as a predictive design framework to optimize processing windows and enable accelerated lifetime testing. Second, this work investigates compositional control and thermal evaporation in CsPbBr 3 thin films. Stepwise isothermal thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) on single-crystal standards establishes a thermodynamic vapor pressure hierarchy (PbBr 2 > CsPb 2 Br 5 > CsPbBr 3 > CsBr). Postdeposition annealing drives the preferential sublimation of unreacted Pb-rich species (PbBr 2 and CsPb 2 Br 5 ) from the film surface, restoring optimal band alignment and surface stoichiometry to yield photovoltaic devices that match stoichiometric controls despite the persistence of Pb-rich species in the bulk. Finally, post-evaporation film quality is enhanced through solvent vapor annealing (SVA) combined with amine functionalization. Exposing co-evaporated CsPbBr 3 thin films to dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) and volatile amine vapors (such as phenethylamine, PEA) induces controlled grain coarsening and passivates interfacial defects. Furthermore, interaction with ambient atmospheric species (CO 2 and H 2 O) mediates the formation of low-dimensional (2D/3D) perovskite heterostructures. Together, these fundamental insights into thermal processing, perovskite reaction kinetics, and chemical surface tailoring provide scalable engineering strategies for high-efficiency, durable all-inorganic perovskite photovoltaics.

content: Some general introductory ideas about suspensions of particles in liquids as well as a set of new findings will be developed in this talk. Suspensions are found in many forms and settings, and the compositions and properties can vary widely. rawEventDetails: Speaker Jeffrey Morris Affiliation The City College of New York Details Event Description Some general introductory ideas about suspensions of particles in liquids as well as a set of new findings will be developed in this talk. Suspensions are found in many forms and settings, and the compositions and properties can vary widely. However, certain issues prevail: one is the influence of the liquid through hydrodynamic interactions, and a second is the importance of the solid fraction and interparticle forces in controlling the flow properties, which we usually call the rheology of the material. Suspensions include colloidal dispersions of nanoparticles as well as cases involving somewhat larger particles such as cement, ceramics, and mud. The last three are all examples of dense suspensions, with solid fraction approaching the limit of flowability known as jamming. Because the rheology most often depends on the magnitude of the applied forces (e.g. pressure gradient in a pipe flow), suspensions are complex fluids – or they may be unyielded soft solids that can be caused to flow by enough force, as seen in the examples of cement mortars or muds. Here, we will present results based on simulations of suspensions approaching jamming to illustrate the unique features of these materials. These include discontinuous shear thickening (DST) as well as shear-induced jamming. The role of interparticle forces, including conservative and frictional contact forces, and the imposed stress in this process will be briefly reviewed, followed by our current examination of structures that are found to be related to the abrupt flow transitions. On approach to jamming, these structures develop as a result of the progressive reduction of the particle degrees of freedom in their motion as networks of contacts are formed. These networks rapidly break and reform during flow, but give rise to strongly correlated near-rigid motions of identifiable domains or “transient clusters.” The resulting fluctuations in motion become dominant as jamming is approached. In the DST regime, the contact number is found to fluctuate very strongly, but can result in highly connected but once again transient structures; system-spanning, or percolating, structures of frictionally-contacting particles are found to have important influence on the observed rheology.

rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Joint CEE/MAE Distinguished Seminar Abstract: This talk will discuss two peculiar effects we recently discovered: the photomolecular effect and the evaporative refrigeration effect. To explain super-thermal solar-interfacial evaporation from hydrogels and other porous materials, we hypothesize that photons can directly cleave off water clusters at the liquid-vapor interface in a way similar to the photoelectric effect, which we call the photomolecular effect. I will discuss experimental evidence we have so far. This photomolecular evaporation process may exist widely in nature. Our studies on photomolecular evaporation also led us to investigate peculiarities in thermal evaporation. At an evaporating interface, a temperature discontinuity exists between the liquid and the vapor sides, which was predicted by theories and observed in some experiments. However, the existing theories cannot explain experiments. We develop a new interfacial condition that can be used to couple transport on both sides of the interface, leading to agreements between theory and experiments. Our modeling reveals the existence of a new refrigeration effect: the vapor temperature can drop below that of the liquid film and in fact, lower than even the condensing surface temperature. This effect has yet to be confirmed experimentally and may find applications in air-conditioning and refrigeration. rawEventDetails: Speaker Ron Weiss Affiliation Massachusetts Institute of Technology Details Event Description Synthetic biology is revolutionizing how we conceptualize and approach the engineering of biological systems. Recent advances in the field are allowing us to expand beyond the construction and analysis of small gene networks towards the implementation of complex multicellular systems with a variety of applications. In this talk I will describe our integrated computational / experimental approach to engineering complex behavior in a variety of cells, with a focus on mammalian cells. In our research, we appropriate design principles from electrical engineering and other established fields. These principles include abstraction, standardization, modularity, and computer aided design. But we also spend considerable effort towards understanding what makes synthetic biology different from all other existing engineering disciplines and discovering new design and construction rules that are effective for this unique discipline. We will briefly describe the implementation of genetic circuits and modules with finely-tuned digital, analog, and multicellular behavior. We will also discuss the generation of a complex tissue from human induced pluripotent stem cells that recapitulates early developmental processes and exhibits a liver bud-like phenotype with integrated vasculature that can be used for drug development and potentially for tissue transplantation. Finally, we will present a mechanism for creation of artificial neural networks that operate in cells using translational regulation, providing a finely tuned mechanism for obtaining non-binary, non-monotonic behaviors with precise amplitude and temporal dynamics and paving the way for cells that can be trained and autonomously learn to perform specific behavioral tasks. content: Ion transport under nanoscale confinement and in the presence of charge is poorly understood from a fundamental perspective. rawEventDetails: Speaker Chinedum Osuji Affiliation University of Pennsylvania Details Event Description Ion transport under nanoscale confinement and in the presence of charge is poorly understood from a fundamental perspective. Under the conditions of dielectric saturation that arise in nanoscale pores, the classical ideas that guide our understanding of electrostatic interactions break down, and new principles that account for the role of pore geometry and chemistry on water structure and ion interactions are needed. At the same time, our ability to develop such principles is hindered by the challenge of generating relevant well-defined geometries that enable experimental studies over statistically meaningful volumes such that experimental data can be more confidently considered alongside data from computational efforts. Beyond the fundamental implications, new understanding is needed to drive the rational design of materials for ion separations in critical minerals production and resource recovery, among other examples, where the need to distinguish between ions of the same valency and charge imposes a severe challenge. Here, we examine transport of ions in polymer membranes with well-defined sub-1 nm pores. The membranes are charged, modestly hydrated nanoporous polymers produced by crosslinking self-assembled lyotropic mesophases with direct hexagonal and gyroid nanostructures. This work addresses the roles of hydration, pore geometry and ion identity on transport using a combination of electrochemical and NMR measurements, and molecular simulation. Our results highlight the roles of hydration, solubility, pore size, and ion-pore wall interactions in dictating transport in the pores. They provide new insight regarding transport under nanoscale confinement in the presence of charge and that we suggest could be relevant for the development of materials for challenging ion separations.

rawEventDetails: Speaker Akshay Gadre Affiliation University of Washington Details Event Description Abstract: Almost every wireless device transmits over the air to communicate, and an increasing fraction of these devices can also use their signals to sense the physical world. As integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) is moving from research into standards, these radios periodically sense the world from the response of the environment on their transmitted signal. At the same time, WiFi, cellular, and automotive platforms are expanding into millimeter-wave spectrum, where wide bandwidths and compact antenna arrays provide fine spatial and temporal resolution, Together, these trends create the foundation for an Internet of Radar Things (IoRT) : a dense population of access points, base stations, vehicles, robots, and mobile devices whose radios can sense while they communicate. Unfortunately, a network of these sensing-capable radios operates largely as n isolated monostatic sensors: each independently occupies spectrum, illuminates an overlapping environment, and retains only the echoes at its own small aperture. These discarded paths contain complementary viewpoints that could extend coverage through occlusions, distinguish physical objects from multipath ghosts, and synthesize apertures far larger than any individual device. This talk presents a unique vision to coordinate these distributed radars coherently to turn this world of radios into one mega-radar. In this talk, we will first present the unique capabilities such a coherent future could enable and how we achieve coherence on commodity off-the-shelf radars to demonstrate these solutions. We specifically show how distributed radars can eliminate ghost artifacts and improve sensing capability, how we can extract material characteristics of objects using this large aperture and how we can use coherence-in-motion to develop free-flowing hand-held imaging solutions for mmWave radars. We further demonstrate how these improvements can directly translate to WiFi and cellular radios. Finally, we end the talk by describing open challenges that still need to be addressed to unleash the true potential of the Internet of Radar Things. Bio: Akshay Gadre is an Assistant Professor at Electrical and Computer Engineering department at the University of Washington. He leads the Networking and Emerging Wireless Technologies (NEWT) Lab at the University of Washington where they explore the upcoming application domains such as satellite IoT, mmWave radars and underwater devices, to apply wireless expertise for improving communication and sensing capability of these devices while preserving the security and privacy of sensor data. Further, the lab explores novel interaction mechanisms for future smart devices such as smart gloves and XR systems using novel force sensing and gaze modalities. His previous research at Carnegie Mellon University operated at the intersection of wireless, mobile and cyber-physical systems with special focus on empowering the low-power Internet-of-Things devices deployed on earth and space. NEWT Lab is also translating these technologies to industry partners including General Motors and IDD Aerospace. His work is published in premier wireless and mobile systems venues including ACM MobiCom, MobiSys, SenSys, Transactions on Sensor Networks and NSDI. Their lab's work has won two best paper awards, four best demo awards, two best-demo runner up awards at these venues. Both Akshay and his students have received the best PhD Forum presentation award at the CPS-IoT Week. Their work has been recognized with the T-Mobile T-Challenge 2024 Most Engaging Presentation Award for their vision of radio digital twins for consumer applications as well as the AFRL SDR University Challenge Best Demo award for developing a cheap SDR platform for exploring satellite networking. While electrocatalysis shares a number of common design principles with thermal catalysis, they also differ greatly. Besides reactivity and selectivity, durability and stability under electrochemical reaction conditions are required for an electrocatalyst. In addition, electrochemical processes often occur at liquid-solid interface under potential, posting new challenges in design. In this presentation, I will discuss our research effort, aiming at uncovering structural design for electrocatalysts. Specifically, I will present the studies on structural and interfacial control of metal oxide and alloy electrocatalysts for oxygen evolution reaction (OER) which occurs in a range of chemical processes, such as hydrogen production from water splitting. Our finding suggests defect engineering is often central in the design of high-performance electrocatalysts for site and crystalline phase tunable complex oxides (i.e., rutile, pyrochlore, and perovskite) and for strained alloys. Flexibility in lattice of complex oxides (A x B y O z ) and tunability of surface strain of alloys often provide the controls of surface and lattice structures that affect the electrocatalytic reaction pathways and performance. Notably, unlike thermal catalysts, proper design of structural defects could simultaneously enhance both activity and stability of electrocatalysts. Valence band analysis, in situ Raman spectroscopy, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, molecular probe and isotope kinetic studies, together with electrochemical characterizations, have been used to identify reactive intermediates and to understand reaction mechanisms.

This raises a fundamental question: How can robustness be quantified when a disturbance changes the probability distribution of system outcomes? content: Robots are being deployed faster and closer to humans, making safety increasingly difficult to quantify and certify. rawEventDetails: Speaker Duy Phuong Nguyen Details Event Description Robots are being deployed faster and closer to humans, making safety increasingly difficult to quantify and certify. Analytical methods often rely on reduced-order models, whereas numerical methods can provide stronger guarantees but quickly become intractable. Learning scales to high-dimensional systems, yet typically offers only empirical or probabilistic assurances. This dissertation combines the scalability of learning with the rigor of control-theoretic safety. In the first part, we develop certifiable safety filters for a designed world with a fixed Operational Design Domain (ODD), which specifies the admissible dynamics, environmental conditions, disturbances, and failure modes. Safety synthesis is formulated as solving a zero-sum game between the robot and an adversary representing the admissible disturbances. We develop a provably convergent adversarial actor–critic method to approximate the game solution and synthesize neural safety policies for high-dimensional systems. This framework enables full-order safety-filter synthesis and zero-shot deployment across different high-dimensional robotic systems. The learned safety value function can also serve as a state–action control barrier function, recovering the maximal robust safety envelope while minimally modifying the task policy. We further show that sufficiently permissive filtering does not degrade asymptotic performance, enabling reinforcement learning that reaches state-of-the-art performance faster than imperfectly safe methods, with zero violations under a perfect filter. Finally, we show that goal-conditioned reach-avoid safety filters make interventions preserve the task rather than only avoid failure, and expand rather than restrict what robots can safely do, from quadruped parkour to underactuated industrial cranes. The second part extends safety beyond the designed world, where the ODD can no longer be held fixed. We first introduce dynamic ODDs, which condition safety values and policies on operating limits inferred and updated at runtime, allowing the robot to adapt as physical conditions change. However, this is not enough when the relevant hazards and failure modes were never specified in advance. We therefore develop an open-context architecture in which generative models interpret the scene, revise the relevant ODD, and select control-grounded safety tools through a representation shared with classical autonomy. This progression lays the foundation for extending certifiable safety from fixed physical envelopes toward open, human-centered autonomy. An embargo has been approved for this thesis. To view a copy of the thesis please stop by the EQUAD Graduate office B209. Adviser: Jaime Fernández Fisac

rawEventDetails: Speaker Rakshit Pathak Details Event Description Machine-perception systems are increasingly deployed at the edge, where they must combine remote sensing (e.g., vision, lidar) with embedded point sensing (e.g., inertial, acoustic, locationing) under tightly constrained energy budgets. Exploiting both forms of sensing requires fusion algorithms that generalize across modalities and tasks, as well as computing platforms that can execute them with high energy efficiency while retaining programmability. This dissertation addresses these needs through algorithm-hardware co-design, spanning the fusion model, processor architecture, silicon prototypes and system infrastructure. First, a generalized Deep-Learning Sensor-Fusion (DL-SF) model is developed, which projects embedded-sensor features into sparse two-dimensional feature maps via domain transformation, scales them to the receptive field of each layer, and concatenates them throughout a convolutional backbone. Across four bookend applications (depth-map generation, 3D human-pose estimation, human trajectory forecasting and human-activity recognition), the DL-SF model improves accuracy and sample efficiency relative to vision-only, early-fusion and late-fusion baselines, for example requiring 3,680 rather than 16k training samples to reach iso-accuracy (98.2%) in activity recognition. Second, the computational structure of the DL-SF model is analyzed to drive the design of a heterogeneous processor in 28nm CMOS, integrating a RISC-V CPU with ISA extensions for embedded-sensor feature extraction, an NVDLA-based convolution accelerator, a Q22.10 fixed-point domain transformation unit, and a memory-data densifier for dense/sparse activation referencing. The prototype executes all four applications end-to-end with 9.3 to 28.1× lower energy and 300 to 500× lower latency than software execution on the CPU, and 15.6 to 24.6× lower energy than reference GPU implementations. Third, this dissertation develops the host-to-chip system infrastructure for a scalable in-memory-computing (IMC) neural-network accelerator in 16nm CMOS, comprising a 4×4 array of IMC cores connected by an on-chip network. This includes the chip interface connecting off-chip signals through the activation and weight buffers to the on-chip network, a PCIe-based FPGA controller using the RIFFA framework, an FPGA emulator of the IMC core for pre-silicon software validation, and a C library that bridges Python-level neural-network mapping tools to the hardware. This infrastructure enabled the measurement and demonstration of CIFAR-10 and ImageNet networks on the prototype. Adviser: Naveen Verma

In this talk, I will highlight how the interplay between carbohydrates and the adaptive and innate arms of the immune response is guiding the development of glycans as vaccine components that act as antigens and immunomodulators. I will also discuss how advances in the field of synthetic glycobiology are enabling the design, engineering, and production of a new generation of carbohydrate-containing vaccine formulations with the potential to prevent infectious diseases and malignancies.

rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Abstract: Thermal conductivity is a basic and familiar property of materials: silver spoons conduct heat well and plastic does not. High thermal conductivity is desirable for heat exchangers and thermal management while low thermal conductivity is needed for thermal insulation. In recent years, the combined efforts of materials scientists, engineers, physicists, and chemists have succeeded in pushing-back long-established limits in the thermal conductivity of materials. Advances in experimental methods have expanded the range of materials that can be studied with high throughput and high accuracy. Theory and computation are playing an increasingly importantrole in guiding and interpreting experiments. In this lecture, I will highlight recent discoveries of extremes of thermal conductivity of materials using examples from hard and soft matter (cubic boron arsenide, ultra-high molecular weight polyethylene, disordered layered 2D materials, functionalized fullerenes) and our work on expanding the upper and lower limits of the thermal conductivity ofcommon polymers (polyurethanes, epoxies, polyesters, and polyimides). Bio: Dr. David Cahill is the Grainger Distinguished Chair in Engineering, and Professor of Materials Science and Engineering at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. He served as department head from 2010 to 2018. His research program advances physical insights on thermal transport at the nanoscale; extremes of low and high thermal conductivity in polymers; thermal metrology for microelectronics;the thermal science of electrochemical cells and battery materials; and materials for quantum computing. Cahill received the 2018 Innovation in Materials Characterization Award of the Materials Research Society, the 2015 Touloukian Award of the American Society of Mechanical Engineers, and the Klemens Award from the International Conference on Phonon Scattering in Condensed Matter. He is a fellow of the MRS, the American Physical Society, the AAAS, and is an elected member of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences. Event Category MAE Departmental Seminars

content: My group engineers genetic systems that accelerate the speed of gene evolution in vivo, enabling us to discover new biomolecular functions and explore sequence-to-function relationships at scale. Bio: Dr. Maruthi Akella is a professor in Aerospace Engineering and Engineering Mechanics at UT Austin where he holds the Cockrell Family Endowed Chair in Engineering. His research encompasses coordinated systems, learning, adaptation, and vision-based sensing. His research group contributed the onboard guidance algorithm for the Intuitive Machines IM-1 mission – the first U.S. moon landing in more than 50 years since the Apollo era. The major impacts of Dr. Akella’s work have been recognized through the AIAA Mechanics and Control of Flight Award, the AAS Dirk Brouwer Award, the IEEE-CSS Award for Excellence in Aerospace Control, the Judith Resnik Space Award from the IEEE Aerospace and Electronic Systems Society, and the AIAA von Kármán Lecture Award in Astronautics. In October 2024, the International Astronomical Union designated asteroid number 5376 – a nearly 5-mile diameter-sized minor planet from the main asteroid belt as “Maruthiakella” honoring Dr. Akella’s contributions to many successful applications in astrodynamics. Dr. Akella is Editor-in Chief for the Journal of the Astronautical Sciences, a Fellow of the AIAA, IEEE, and AAS, and holds the Academician rank with the International Academy of Astronautics. rawEventDetails: Speaker Alfredo Alexander-Katz Affiliation Massachusetts Institute of Technology Details Event Description Single chain nanoparticles (SCNPs) are small globules composed typically of a single random heteropolymer (RHP) chain containing 2 or more chemistries. In the past two decades, there have been significant advances in controlling the properties of these SCNPs in order to convert such seemingly inert globules into chemical reactors. More recently, however, RHPs have been used in many other applications such as protein protectants, catalysis, membrane active polymers, as well as chaperon-like biomimetic polymers. Many of these properties were believed to be only possible with sequence-defined natural peptides, and it is of interest to understand how RHPs are able to achieve these functions. Here, we will present our in-silico work on how RHPs are arranged at the molecular level and highlight under what conditions one expects these polymers to present some of the interfacial properties proteins display. In particular, we will put special attention to the thermodynamics of globule formation in the presence of multiple chemistries, and the effect of Flory interaction parameters between the different species. As will be shown, under some conditions, these globules are able to exhibit a key biological property called hydration frustration, where some hydrophilic groups are dehydrated and buried while some hydrophobic groups are exposed at the water interface of the globule. This frustrated state is the basis of protein function and we believe this property to be critical in the future development of single chain nanoparticle for biological or biomimetic applications. We will finalize with a perspective on how RHPs interact with proteins, and potential avenues for utilizing them for controlling certain biological processes.

rawEventDetails: Speaker Yuhao Zhu Affiliation University of Rochester Details Event Description Abstract: Computers are increasingly integrated into embodied systems that operate in complex real-world environments, such as autonomous robots and smart wearable/Extended Reality (XR) glasses. These systems must continuously sense and interpret the physical world while also generating information that engages human perceptual and cognitive systems. This talk argues that programming and architecting future computer systems must integrate sensing and human cognition into the computing stack, and presents my lab’s work toward this vision. First, I will discuss the co-design of sensing and computation, where we design novel computational image sensors and compile visual programs across heterogeneous sensing and computing hardware. Second, I will discuss co-optimizing computing with humans, where we build novel computational models of human visual perception that provide perceptual, not numerical, specifications and constraints for navigating the enormous design space of visual programs. Together, these projects point toward an exciting future of computing that jointly reasons about machines, the physical world, and human cognition. Bio: Yuhao Zhu is an Associate Professor of Computer Science, Brain and Cognitive Sciences, and an Asaro Biggar Family Fellow in Data Science, all at University of Rochester, where he and his students are mostly drawn to research problems at the intersection of computer architecture, sensing, and human factors. rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Abstract: Nuclear electric propulsion (NEP) offers the potential to fundamentally expand the capability and reach of spacecraft, but realizing that potential requires overcoming significant challenges in reactor technology, power conversion and distribution, thermal management, electric propulsion, and system integration. This seminar will examine the current state of NEP development, highlighting recent progress while exploring the demanding requirements associated with operating high-power systems continuously for years or even decades in the space environment. Particular attention will be given to high-power electric propulsion, lightweight high-temperature radiators, radiation-tolerant power electronics, and the testing and evaluation infrastructure needed to mature these technologies and demonstrate integrated systems. The discussion will also consider an evolutionary path toward increasingly capable NEP systems, beginning with lower-power long-duration missions and building toward higher-power systems for human exploration and deep-space science. Finally, the seminar will examine the technology investments and national test and evaluation capabilities needed to turn this vision into a sustained spaceflight capability. BIO : Dr. Kurt Polzin is a senior aerospace engineer and internationally recognized expert in advanced space propulsion. He is from the George C. Marshall Space Flight Center and currently serves as NASA’s Capability Manager for Advanced Propulsion within the Space Transportation Program, where he leads technology development activities spanning electric propulsion, green propellants, solar sails, and other advanced propulsion technologies. Previously, he served as Chief Engineer for NASA’s Space Nuclear Propulsion portfolio as the engineering technical authority for a national, multi-agency effort to advance nuclear thermal and nuclear electric propulsion systems. Dr. Polzin has authored more than 150 technical publications and has conducted research and development in electric propulsion, plasma physics, nuclear propulsion, spacecraft power systems, and advanced space transportation. He is an AIAA Fellow and recipient of the AIAA Engineer of the Year and Plasmadynamics & Lasers Awards. Dr. Polzin received his B.S. in Aerospace Engineering from The Ohio State University and his M.A. and Ph.D. in Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering from Princeton University. rawEventDetails: Speaker Danielle Mai Affiliation Stanford University Details Event Description Evolution allows organisms to adapt to their environments, yet some molecular patterns stay constant through billions of years of evolution. These patterns encode the secrets of biological materials, such that similar patterns often emerge in different materials with similar functions. For example, a family of elastin proteins form stretchable fibers, which allow the constant movement of human skin, blood vessels, and lungs. We aim to decode the secrets of biological materials by investigating sequence patterns in repetitive proteins, towards establishing systematic protein sequence–biomaterial property relationships. This talk explores two classes of repetitive proteins as stimuli-responsive biopolymers. First, we investigate bacterial proteins that undergo conformational changes in response to calcium ions. We modify hydrophobicity, electrostatics, and sequence heterogeneity to demonstrate sequence-dependent, reversible folding and domain size changes in response to calcium ions. We also identify structural features that give rise to ion selectivity, which is not yet well-predicted by AI/ML tools. Second, we introduce enzymatic stimuli to drive isothermal phase separation of elastin-like polypeptides (ELPs). ELPs have drawn interest as heat-responsive biopolymers, such that ELPs undergo reversible phase separation from water upon heating. However, temperature is not always a convenient trigger, especially in biological environments that maintain near-constant temperature, pH, and ionic composition. To expand ELP function, we program a mechanism for isothermal phase separation upon proteolytic cleavage of a di-block ELP. This mechanism presents a new opportunity to exploit biological triggers for ELP phase behavior and self-assembly processes. Overall, we demonstrate repetitive proteins as tunable and modular building blocks for functional biomaterials.

Bio: Timothy Barfoot (University of Toronto Institute for Aerospace Studies – UTIAS) works in the area of autonomy for mobile robots targeting a variety of applications. He develops methods (localization, mapping, planning, control) to allow robots to operate over long periods of time in large-scale, unstructured, three-dimensional environments, using rich onboard sensing (e.g., cameras, laser rangefinders, radar) and computation. Timothy holds a BASc (9T6+PEY, Aerospace Option) from the UofT Engineering Science program and a PhD from UTIAS in robotics. He took up his academic position at UTIAS in May 2007, after spending four years at MDA Space (builder of the well-known Canadarm space manipulators), where he developed autonomous vehicle navigation technologies for both planetary rovers and terrestrial applications such as underground mining. He is a Fellow of the IEEE, a Fellow of the Canadian Academy of Engineering, held a Canada Research Chair for the full 10 years, was an Early Researcher Awardee in the Province of Ontario, and has received three paper awards at the IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA 2010, 2021, 2025) as well as four at the Conference on Robots and Vision (CRV 2014, 2016, 2023, 2025). Timothy began serving as Director (Dept. Head) of UTIAS on 1 July 2026, and previously served as Director of the UofT Robotics Institute,Director of the UofT Collaborative Specialization in Robotics, co-Faculty Advisor of UofT's self-driving car team that won the SAE Autodrivecompetition several times, Chair of the UofT Engineering Science Robotics Major, and was a Faculty Affiliate of the Vector Institute. rawEventDetails: Details Event Description How is it possible that 1/4 of the Nobel Prizes in Physics since 2006 have been for astrophysics? All 5 of them came from new technologies, and two required space observatories. I’ll review the breakthrough ideas that grew into discoveries, and suggest where future technologies might go.The JWST is working brilliantly, and has found Little Red Dots, the current mystery object. But there’s still no Earth 2.0. The DKIST solar telescope with adaptive optics is working beautifully. The Vera Rubin Telescope is online, the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope will be launched just before this colloquium to study dark matter, dark energy, and exoplanets, and the 39 m diameter Extremely Large Telescope will be doing science around 2030. Among the new possibilities: the Habitable Worlds Observatory, a workhorse UV-near IR observatory with a coronagraph for exoplanets, and X-ray and far IR observatories from Probe class ($1B) to flagships. New detector and mirror technologies are making both exciting. The NAUTILUS concept will use molded glass lenses up to 8 m in diameter in space to collect light for spectroscopy. We’re also developing hybrid observatories combining telescopes and interferometers on the ground with satellites. The Landolt absolute photometric calibrator beacon will fly in 2029, and the CELESTE mission is a proposed Small Explorer to offer a laser beacon for adaptive optics to the ELT, giving it diffraction-limited image quality at visible wavelengths where the sky is darkest. An orbiting starshade could cast a star shadow on the ELT and enable imaging of another Earth in one minute. The Black Hole Explorer would extend the Event Horizon Telescope with an orbiting antenna could measure the spin of a black hole. If you can imagine it, you can build it.
